seoTitle: How to Create a Namecheap Email for Your Website
metaDescription: Create a professional Namecheap email for your website in 2026: compare Private Email plans, create a mailbox, and point the MX records so mail arrives.
intro: A free @gmail or @outlook address doesn't do much for a business site, which is why pairing your domain with Namecheap's Private Email service is worth the small monthly cost. This guide covers picking a plan sized to how many mailboxes you need, creating your first mailbox once you've bought one, and the DNS step that's easy to skip and is the actual reason a new mailbox sometimes never receives mail.
prerequisites: A domain already added to your Namecheap account (or one you can point at Namecheap's mail servers)
An active Private Email subscription for that domain — this is billed separately from domain registration or hosting
costNote: Private Email is a paid add-on, not something bundled free with a Namecheap domain, though every plan carries a 30-day free trial. At the time of recording, promotional first-year pricing ran from $11.88/year for Starter (1 mailbox) up to $47.88/year for Ultimate (5 mailboxes); each tier renews at a higher rate in year two, listed in the table below.

steps.heading: Compare the Private Email plans
steps.body: Namecheap's Private Email pricing page lists three tiers: Starter with 1 mailbox and 5GB, Pro with 3 mailboxes and 30GB plus full mobile sync, and Ultimate with 5 mailboxes, 75GB, mobile sync, Docs/Sheets/Presentations, and Premium Email Delivery (Ultimate's mail is sent from separate high-reputation servers). Docs, Sheets & Presentations is included from Pro upward, not only on Ultimate. Each card shows a promotional first-term price next to a smaller renewal price — check the renewal figure, since that's what recurs from year two onward. Namecheap also offers a custom plan, reachable through Get in touch, for anyone needing more than 50 mailboxes or Private Email on more than 20 domains.

image.caption: The three Private Email pricing tiers — Starter, Pro, and Ultimate — each listing mailbox count, storage, and included features.

steps.heading: Find your domain in the Namecheap dashboard
steps.body: After purchasing, your domain shows up under Domain List in the left-hand dashboard menu, marked Active with domain privacy protection noted underneath it. Clicking Manage on the domain leads into its DNS and email settings. This is one valid route to Private Email; the sidebar also has a Private Email link that goes there more directly, covered in the next step.

image.caption: The Domain List screen showing an active domain with privacy protection on, and a Manage link to open its settings.

steps.heading: Open Private Email Subscriptions
steps.body: Click Private Email in the dashboard's left sidebar to reach Private Email Subscriptions, which lists your domain, its plan, status, whether auto-renew is on, and the exact expiration date. Confirm the subscription reads Active before trying to create a mailbox. A lapsed or still-pending subscription blocks mailbox creation even though the domain itself keeps showing as active, and that mismatch is a common source of confusion.

image.caption: The Private Email Subscriptions list, showing the domain's plan, active status, auto-renew toggle, and expiration date.

steps.heading: Create your first mailbox
steps.body: From the subscription's management screen, click Create Mailbox to open a form asking for a Mailbox Name (the part before the @ sign), a password, a password confirmation, and how much of the plan's total storage to assign to this mailbox. Namecheap doesn't require setting up every included mailbox right away — create one now and add the rest whenever you need them. If the button reads Buy Mailbox instead of Create Mailbox, every mailbox slot on the plan is already used and an additional one needs to be purchased first.

image.caption: The Create Mailbox dialog, asking for a mailbox name, password, and how much storage to assign from the plan's total.

steps.heading: Set a strong password and save
steps.body: Clicking into the password field, a browser password manager may offer to generate and store a strong random one, which is a sensible option for anything not typed from memory day to day, like a shared support inbox. Re-enter the same password in Confirm Password; a short random string is easy to mistype once, and the form flags a mismatch immediately rather than after Save Changes is clicked. Click Save Changes to finish and activate the mailbox.

image.caption: The Create Mailbox form filled in, with Google Password Manager offering to generate a strong password for the new mailbox.

steps.heading: Point the domain's MX records so mail arrives
steps.body: Private Email needs two MX records: mx1.privateemail.com and mx2.privateemail.com, both at priority 10. If the domain runs on Namecheap's own nameservers, open Advanced DNS, scroll to Mail Settings, and choose Private Email from the dropdown, which writes both records for you. If DNS is hosted elsewhere (Cloudflare, GoDaddy, a previous host), those same two records need to be added manually in that provider's panel, and any old MX records from a prior email provider should be removed first. Namecheap checks for the record every 15 minutes and activates the subscription once it's detected, though propagation can take up to 4 hours. For subscriptions bought from June 2026 onward, a DKIM record (host privateemail._domainkey) is also available immediately and is worth adding alongside SPF so outgoing mail is less likely to land in spam.

steps.heading: Connect the mailbox to Gmail or Outlook
steps.body: Once the mailbox exists, either use Namecheap's webmail directly or connect the address to a client already in daily use. Gmail's "Add another email address" option under Accounts settings, and the equivalent "Add account" flow in Outlook, both accept the IMAP or POP settings Namecheap lists on the mailbox's management page. That means checking the domain's mail doesn't require a separate inbox habit just because the address lives outside Gmail's own servers.

troubleshooting.problem: "Buy Mailbox" shows up instead of "Create Mailbox"
troubleshooting.cause: Every mailbox slot included in the current plan is already in use.
troubleshooting.fix: Purchase an additional mailbox for the subscription, then create the new address.

troubleshooting.problem: Save Changes rejects the new mailbox with a password mismatch
troubleshooting.cause: The Mailbox Password and Confirm Password fields don't match, which is easy to trigger with a long generated password typed or pasted twice.
troubleshooting.fix: Use the password manager's autofill for both fields, or copy the generated password once and paste it into each field instead of retyping it.

troubleshooting.problem: The mailbox sends mail but never seems to receive any
troubleshooting.cause: MX records still point at a previous email provider, or the two Private Email MX records (mx1/mx2.privateemail.com, priority 10) were never added on a third-party DNS host.
troubleshooting.fix: Add or correct both MX records in the domain's DNS panel, remove any conflicting old MX records, and allow up to 4 hours for propagation and Namecheap's verification check.

troubleshooting.problem: Outgoing mail lands in recipients' spam folders
troubleshooting.cause: No SPF or DKIM record is set for the domain, so receiving mail servers can't confirm the mail came from Namecheap's servers.
troubleshooting.fix: Add the SPF record and, for subscriptions from June 2026 onward, the DKIM record at privateemail._domainkey, following Namecheap's DNS setup guide for the domain's specific nameserver situation.

faq.question: Which DNS records does Namecheap Private Email need?
faq.answer: Two MX records, mx1.privateemail.com and mx2.privateemail.com, both at priority 10. Domains on Namecheap's own nameservers can add both at once from Advanced DNS's Mail Settings dropdown; third-party DNS hosts need them added by hand.

faq.question: Can I use my custom domain email in Gmail or Outlook?
faq.answer: Yes. Once the mailbox is created, connect it in Gmail or Outlook using the IMAP or POP settings listed on the mailbox's management page in Namecheap.

faq.question: Do I have to create all my mailboxes at once?
faq.answer: No. Namecheap doesn't require setting up every mailbox included in a plan right away; set up what's needed now and create the rest later.

faq.question: Why does "Buy Mailbox" appear instead of "Create Mailbox"?
faq.answer: It means the plan's mailbox slots are all used. An additional mailbox has to be purchased before another one can be created.

faq.question: How long does it take for a new mailbox to start receiving mail?
faq.answer: Namecheap checks the domain's MX records every 15 minutes and activates the subscription once they're detected, but full DNS propagation can take up to 4 hours, longer in rare cases.

faq.question: Are the plans still called Starter, Pro, and Ultimate?
faq.answer: Mostly, yes, though Namecheap has begun rolling out a rebuilt Private Email platform since June 2026 and lists the same tiers under new names in places (Launch, Expand, and Scale Mail) at identical per-mailbox prices. Expect either set of names depending on when the account or subscription was created.
